\chapter{Communication Complexity — Func Equality}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.DeterministicCC.FuncEquality
\section{Overview}

This module establishes the exact deterministic communication complexity of the
equality function on $n$-bit strings and provides a public-coin upper bound via
universal hashing.  The two headline results are: the deterministic complexity
equals $0$ when $n = 0$ and $n + 1$ otherwise; and the public-coin complexity is
at most $\lceil \log_2(\lceil \varepsilon^{-1} \rceil + 1)\rceil + 1$ for any
error tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Equality function on $n$-bit strings]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput}
For a natural number $n$, \texttt{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality}
is the Boolean function
$\mathrm{equality}_n : \mathrm{BoolInput}\,n \times \mathrm{BoolInput}\,n \to \mathrm{Bool}$
that returns \texttt{true} if and only if Alice's input $x$ equals Bob's input $y$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Hash space for the equality protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.HashSpace}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.HashSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Hash.HashSpace}
$\mathrm{HashSpace}(n, k)$ is the type of all hash functions from $n$-bit strings
into $\mathrm{Fin}(2^k)$; it serves as the public-randomness space for the
hashing-based equality protocol.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Deterministic complexity upper bound for equality]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.communicationComplexity_le}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.communicationComplexity_le}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity_le_clog_card_X_alpha, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality}
\difficulty{4}
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
\[
  D(\mathrm{equality}_n) \;\le\; n + 1.
\]
This follows from the naive protocol in which Alice transmits her entire $n$-bit
input and Bob sends back the single comparison bit.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Deterministic complexity of equality at $n = 0$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.communicationComplexity_zero}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.communicationComplexity_zero}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity_le_iff, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality}
\difficulty{4}
When $n = 0$ both inputs are the unique empty string, so the equality function
is constantly \texttt{true} and requires zero communication:
\[
  D(\mathrm{equality}_0) = 0.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Deterministic complexity lower bound for equality]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.le_communicationComplexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.le_communicationComplexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.le_communicationComplexity_of_forall_lt_ncard, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.monoPartition_cross_mem, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.monoPartition_point_mem, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.monoPartition_values_eq}
\difficulty{6}
For every $n \ge 1$,
\[
  n + 1 \;\le\; D(\mathrm{equality}_n).
\]
The key argument is that any monochromatic rectangle that contains a diagonal
pair $(x, x)$ must equal the singleton $\{(x,x)\}$, so any valid partition
of the input matrix into monochromatic rectangles contains at least $2^n + 1$
pieces, requiring $n + 1$ bits to index.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exact deterministic complexity of equality]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.communicationComplexity_eq}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.communicationComplexity_eq}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.communicationComplexity_le, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.communicationComplexity_zero, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.le_communicationComplexity}
\difficulty{4}
The deterministic communication complexity of the equality function on $n$-bit
strings is
\[
  D(\mathrm{equality}_n) \;=\; \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } n = 0, \\ n + 1 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Equality hashing protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.HashSpace, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.alice, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.bob, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.output}
$\mathrm{equalityHashProtocol}(n, k)$ is the standard public-coin protocol for
equality in which, given a shared random hash $h \in \mathrm{HashSpace}(n, k)$,
Alice sends $h(x) \in \mathrm{Fin}(2^k)$ and Bob replies with
$\mathtt{decide}(h(y) = h(x))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Run semantics of the equality hashing protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol_rrun}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol_rrun}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.HashSpace, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.rrun}
\difficulty{3}
For all $x, y : \mathrm{BoolInput}\,n$ and $h : \mathrm{HashSpace}(n,k)$,
\[
  (\mathrm{equalityHashProtocol}\,n\,k).\mathrm{rrun}\,x\,y\,h
  \;=\; \mathtt{decide}(h(x) = h(y)).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Complexity of the equality hashing protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol_complexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol_complexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.alice, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.bob, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.output}
\difficulty{4}
The worst-case communication cost of $\mathrm{equalityHashProtocol}(n, k)$ is
exactly $k + 1$ bits.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Public-coin upper bound for equality via hash parameter]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.publicCoin_communicationComplexity_le_of_hε}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.publicCoin_communicationComplexity_le_of_hε}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.HashSpace, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol_complexity, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equalityHashProtocol_rrun, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Hash.collision_prob_le, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.rrun, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.communicationComplexity_le_of_finiteMessage}
\difficulty{4}
If $\varepsilon > 0$ and $1/2^k < \varepsilon$, then the public-coin
communication complexity of $\mathrm{equality}_n$ with error at most $\varepsilon$
satisfies
\[
  R_\varepsilon(\mathrm{equality}_n) \;\le\; k + 1.
\]
The error bound follows from the collision probability of the random hash family.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Public-coin upper bound for equality via $\varepsilon$]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.publicCoin_communicationComplexity_le}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.publicCoin_communicationComplexity_le}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.publicCoin_communicationComplexity_le_of_hε, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.communicationComplexity}
\difficulty{5}
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$,
\[
  R_\varepsilon(\mathrm{equality}_n)
  \;\le\; \left\lfloor \log_2\!\left(\lceil \varepsilon^{-1} \rceil + 1\right)\right\rfloor + 1.
\]
\end{theorem}
